title: Memory Garden
subtitle: A journey to rediscover forgotten moments
medicalDisclaimer: Memory Garden is a light practice game for attention and working memory. It is not intended for medical diagnosis and cannot replace a professional assessment.

steps.title: A Fog Has Settled
steps.text: Grandma, a little fog has drifted into our garden — some flowers are harder to see now. But that's okay, we'll take our time.
steps.sub: Relax and take a deep breath...

steps.title: Remember This Flower
steps.text: Flowers will bloom one after another. Please look at each one carefully.
steps.sub: Each flower will linger for a moment

steps.title: Finding the Shadow of Memory
steps.text: If you see a flower that looks exactly like one from "before"...
steps.sub: That means a memory has returned!

steps.title: Press the Button
steps.text: When you notice a flower repeating, gently press the « Déjà vu » button.
steps.sub: It's okay if you miss one — we're just taking a stroll.

s1.title: 1. Product Nature
s1.content: Memory Garden is a cognitive training entertainment application based on the N-back paradigm. This product aims to help users practice working memory through gamification. It is an educational entertainment product, not a medical device, and is not intended for diagnosing, treating, mitigating, or preventing any disease or medical condition.

s2.title: 2. Scientific Basis
s2.content: This product's training methodology is based on the N-back working memory training paradigm from cognitive psychology. Since Wayne Kirchner first proposed it in 1958, this paradigm has been widely used in cognitive psychology research. However, regarding the transfer effects of N-back training to other cognitive abilities, there remains scientific debate:
s2.li1: Jaeggi et al. (2008) claimed that dual N-back training could improve fluid intelligence, but subsequent studies have presented different viewpoints.
s2.li2: A comprehensive review by Simons et al. (2017) concluded that cognitive training effects are mainly limited to the training task itself, with insufficient evidence for transfer to other cognitive abilities.

s3.title: 3. Not a Substitute for Professional Advice
s3.content: This product cannot replace professional assessment, diagnosis, or advice from doctors, therapists, cognitive rehabilitation specialists, or other healthcare professionals. If you have concerns about cognitive health, please consult a qualified healthcare professional.

s4.title: 4. No Guarantee of Results
s4.content: The effects of cognitive training vary among individuals. This product does not guarantee any specific training outcomes or cognitive improvement. Training results are influenced by multiple factors, including but not limited to training frequency, baseline cognitive ability, age, and health status.

s5.title: 5. Intended Audience
s5.content: This product is recommended for users aged 8 and above. Children under 8 should use this product under the guidance of a parent or guardian. This product does not knowingly collect personal information from children under 8.

s6.title: 6. Use at Your Own Risk
s6.content: Users understand and agree that any results arising from the use of this product (including but not limited to training effects, cognitive changes, etc.) are borne solely by the user. The developer shall not be liable for any direct, indirect, incidental, special, or consequential damages arising from the use or inability to use this product.

s1.title: 1. What is the N-back Task?
s1.p1: N-back is a classic Working Memory (WM) assessment and training paradigm, proposed by Wayne Kirchner in 1958. It belongs to the continuous performance task family.
s1.p2: Basic principle: Participants continuously monitor a series of stimuli (such as letters, positions, graphics) and judge whether the current stimulus matches the one presented n steps back. The "n" value represents the difficulty level (e.g., 1-back, 2-back, 3-back). A larger n means higher working memory load.
s1.p3: Single N-back processes only one modality (e.g., visual positions or auditory letters); Dual N-back processes two modalities simultaneously (visual + auditory), making it harder and commonly used in training research.
s1.li1: Single N-back: processes only one modality (e.g., visual positions or auditory letters)
s1.li2: Dual N-back: processes two modalities simultaneously (visual + auditory); participants must judge both position and letter matches n steps back
s1.p4: Tasks are typically adaptive: n value increases when performance is good and decreases when poor, maintaining the challenge.

s2.title: 2. What Problems Does It Solve?
s2.p1: Working memory is the ability to store and manipulate information in the short term. It is the core of cognition, closely related to attention, learning, reasoning, and problem-solving. N-back training primarily addresses:
s2.p2: Helps improve information updating, maintenance, and the ability to suppress irrelevant information.
s2.p3: Improves cognitive control and conflict resolution (e.g., Stroop task).
s2.li1: ADHD (Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder): improves verbal working memory
s2.li3: Healthy adults: enhances daily memory and learning efficiency
s2.p4: May improve Fluid Intelligence (Gf) — the ability for abstract reasoning and solving novel problems, as opposed to crystallized intelligence (learned knowledge).

s3.title: 3. Why Does It Work? Mechanisms and Evidence
s3.li1: N-back requires continuous updating of working memory content, suppressing old information, and switching attention, training core executive functions
s3.li2: Dual N-back involves multiple modalities, potentially simulating more complex cognitive demands and enhancing transfer potential
s3.p1: Nearly all studies show significant improvement in training task performance itself (near transfer to similar N-back tasks).
s3.li3: Near transfer: moderate effect to other working memory tasks (e.g., running memory, digit span)
s3.li4: Far transfer: to fluid intelligence, attention, executive function, etc., small effect (Hedges' g ≈ 0.16–0.24)
s3.li5: Some studies show superiority over other methods like memory palaces, especially in transfer to untrained tasks
s3.p2: May increase prefrontal activity, enhance P300 component, expand attentional focus capacity.
s3.li7: Far transfer effects are small and inconsistent, influenced by control group type (active vs. passive), training dosage, and individual differences
s3.li8: Improvements may partly stem from strategy learning (e.g., chunking) rather than pure capacity increase
s3.li9: Not a cure-all: short-term training effects are limited, long-term persistence is more important

s4.title: 4. Key Papers and References
s4.ref1: Jaeggi, S. M., et al. (2008). Improving fluid intelligence with training on working memory. PNAS. First reported that dual N-back training significantly improved fluid intelligence, sparking widespread attention.
s4.ref2: Au et al. (2015): supports small Gf improvement
s4.ref3: Soveri et al. (2017): near transfer moderate, far transfer small
s4.ref4: Chinese-language studies have explored the potential of mobile-app dual N-back to improve visuospatial working memory and executive functions such as the Stroop task
s4.ref5: Related applied studies in adolescents and adults with ADHD
s4.p1: Search PubMed / Google Scholar for "dual n-back training" or "N-back working memory training". Practice advice: start from 2-back, 15–20 minutes daily for several weeks. Combining feedback and adaptive difficulty yields better results.
s4.summary: Summary: N-back is a scientifically validated working memory training tool. Near transfer is reliable, far transfer has potential but with moderate effects. Suitable for daily cognitive maintenance and rehabilitation support. Persistence and personalized adjustment are key. Effects vary by individual, and combining with other cognitive training or lifestyle changes may be even better.
